transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, my regular doctor wanted me to come in, mostly. She seems concerned that my meal planning has gotten, in her words, too tight or too controlled. I don’t quite see it that way, honestly. To me it’s more that I have a routine that keeps the day orderly.

I usually keep breakfast simple, like yogurt, and then if I’m busy I may just skip lunch because I’m working or out running errands and it doesn’t feel necessary at the time. Then dinner is very measured—planned out, not random—because I like knowing where the day is going and not having things feel chaotic. I suppose she thinks it’s become too narrow, but from my perspective it’s just structure.
Do you follow this routine because you're concerned about gaining weight or because you feel better when you control your food intake in terms of how you see yourself or your body shape?

I suppose… yes, there is a weight part to it, though I don’t like saying it that way because it sounds so blunt. It’s not as if I’m sitting there thinking about it dramatically all day, but if I’ve had what I’d consider a normal dinner, or if I’ve eaten out at a restaurant where I can’t measure things the way I usually do, and then the scale is up even a pound the next morning, I get this very sharp feeling of panic.

It feels like I’ve done something wrong, or like I’ve let things get away from me. I know one pound doesn’t sound like much, and logically I can tell myself it might just be salt or timing or whatever, but emotionally it feels like I’ve lost control. Then I feel like I need to correct it the next day, get things back where they should be. So yes, I guess controlling the food is tied to feeling okay about my body and not feeling like I’m slipping.

After eating a meal that you didn’t plan or measure, like at a restaurant, do you ever make yourself vomit, take laxatives, or exercise more than usual to try to 'undo' the food or prevent weight gain?

I don’t think so… not in the way you mean. I mean, I don’t make myself vomit. That’s never been something I do. And laxatives—no, not for that. I’m a little uncomfortable even saying it because it sounds so extreme, but no, that isn’t part of what I do.

The exercise part is harder for me to answer cleanly, because if I feel unsettled after a meal I didn’t plan, I might be more restless the next day or want to be more “back on track,” but I wouldn’t say I have some formal punishment routine where I go and exercise for hours to erase it. It’s more that I get anxious and want things orderly again. But vomiting or taking things to undo food, no.

Has this way of managing your food and weight affected your daily life in any important ways, like causing you a lot of stress, making it hard to be flexible, or affecting your relationships or activities?

It has, yes… though I tend to tell myself it hasn’t because I’m still functioning. I still do my analysis work, and I keep up with errands and appointments and the ordinary things that need to get done. So on paper, I suppose it doesn’t look like everything has fallen apart or anything like that.

But the flexibility part is where it shows up. I’ve mostly stopped joining friends for meals after book club, for example. We used to go out afterward, nothing elaborate, just dinner or something small, and now I usually find a reason not to go. I’ll say I’m tired or I have something to do the next morning, but really it’s because it throws off the plan I’m relying on. I don’t know what the portions will be, or what’s in things, or how it fits into the rest of the day, and then I spend the whole time feeling tense instead of enjoying being with people.

So… yes, I guess it has narrowed things. Not in every area, but socially, especially around meals, I’ve pulled back more than I like to admit.
Outside of concerns about food, weight, or meal planning, do you find yourself feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t think I would describe myself as hopeless, no. That sounds stronger than what I recognize in myself. I have days where I feel discouraged or sort of worn out by how much mental space all of this takes up, but outside of the food and planning part, I don’t know that I’m walking around feeling depressed in a general way.

As for losing interest… I mean, I still like the things I like, at least in principle. I still read, I still go to book club, I still care about my work being done properly. Sometimes I don’t enjoy things as freely as I used to, but it’s hard for me to separate whether that’s a mood problem or whether it’s because so many activities seem to end up involving food or restaurants or timing meals, and then I get tense.

So I guess my answer is… not really in a broad, across-the-board way. I wouldn’t say I feel hopeless. I feel restricted, maybe, or preoccupied. But not exactly down in the way I think you’re asking.
Do you ever feel guilty or feel like you've failed yourself because of what or how much you eat, even if it's something most people wouldn't think twice about?

Yes… I do, though I might not use the word “guilty” right away. It’s more like I feel I’ve let myself get sloppy, or that I’ve failed at keeping myself in hand. And I know how that sounds at my age—I’m 63, I’m not trying to look like a young woman, and I’m not under any illusion that I should look the way I did decades ago.

But I still notice my waist and hips in my clothes more than I’d like to admit. If something feels snug, or if I look in the mirror and feel like those areas aren’t… contained, I suppose is the word, then I get this immediate sense that I’ve done something wrong. Even if the meal itself was perfectly ordinary, something most people would just eat and move on from.

It’s not always about the exact food, I guess. It’s what the food seems to mean afterward—whether I’m managing myself properly, whether I’ve kept control. And if my clothes don’t feel right, then I can very quickly decide I’ve failed, even if, rationally, I know that’s a harsh way to judge one meal or one day.
Have you ever had periods of time where you felt down or low most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks at a time?

I don’t think so… not in that clear, sustained way you’re describing. I’ve had low days, certainly, and sometimes a run of days where I feel more worn down or discouraged than usual. But if you mean most of the day, almost every day, for two weeks or more, I’m not sure I can point to a period like that.

I tend to keep moving through things—work, errands, the usual obligations—so sometimes I’m not even sure I’d notice it properly unless it stopped me. But “down most of the day” sounds more constant than what I experience. Mine feels more like… spells of feeling depleted or frustrated, and then I can still get absorbed in a task or a book or something practical.

So I’d say no, not really. Or at least not that I recognize as a two-week stretch like that.
Have you noticed any effects on your work performance or physical health because of your concerns about food and control over your eating?

I think… mostly I’m still functioning, if that’s what you mean. I mean, I still get my analysis work done. I’m careful about deadlines and checking things, and I don’t think anyone at work would say I’m suddenly unreliable or anything like that. And I still manage errands and the practical things—groceries, appointments, paying bills, all of that.

Where it has changed things is more socially, I suppose. After book club, people often want to go for a meal or even just something casual, and I used to go along more easily. Now I’ve mostly stopped doing that, because it throws off the plan I rely on for eating. It’s not that I don’t want to see them, exactly. I do. I like them. But if the timing is different, or I don’t know what the options will be, or it means eating something I hadn’t accounted for, I get very tense about it.

So I wouldn’t say my work has fallen apart or that I can’t take care of myself physically in the day-to-day sense. But it has narrowed things. I’m much more likely to go to book club and then leave, rather than join everyone afterward, because it feels safer to stick to what I had planned.

Have your concerns about food, weight, or control over eating caused you significant distress or affected any other important areas of your life, such as your ability to focus at work, take care of personal matters, or engage in hobbies?

Yes, it has, though I suppose I’d say it’s more… contained than dramatic. I still keep up with my analysis work. I’m not missing deadlines or letting things pile up in some obvious way, and I still manage my errands and the ordinary personal matters—shopping, appointments, bills, that sort of thing.

But it does affect my life around the edges, and maybe those edges are bigger than I like to admit. The main thing is book club. I still go, because I enjoy the books and the discussion, and I don’t want to become someone who stops doing things altogether. But afterward, when people suggest getting a meal or going somewhere for a bite, I’ve mostly stopped joining them.

It’s not because I dislike them. I actually feel a bit sad about it, because I like the conversation afterward too. But eating out like that throws off the plan I rely on, and then I spend the whole time thinking about what I’m supposed to have, what I didn’t account for, whether I’ll feel out of control afterward. So it feels easier and safer to just go home.

So, no, my work and errands haven’t really suffered in a visible way. But socially, yes—it’s narrowed what I’m willing to do.

Do you feel driven to control your eating because of intrusive, unwanted thoughts about food or weight, or do you do it more because you feel anxious or uncomfortable if things aren’t planned and measured just right?

I think it’s more the second thing, honestly. I wouldn’t say it’s like intrusive thoughts in the sense of thoughts barging in that feel separate from me, if that makes sense. It’s more that if the day isn’t planned around food in a fairly exact way, I feel unsettled—like I’ve lost the structure of the day.

I came in because my doctor seems concerned that my meal planning has gotten too tight. To me, it still feels sort of practical and orderly. Breakfast is usually just yogurt, because it’s simple and I know what it is. If I’m busy, lunch can get skipped, which doesn’t feel like a big decision at the time—it’s more that I’m working or out doing things and it seems easier not to interrupt everything. Then dinner is very measured, because by then I want the day to feel… contained, I suppose. Like I can account for it.

So no, I don’t experience it as unwanted thoughts attacking me exactly. It’s more that I feel anxious or uncomfortable when I can’t keep it planned and measured properly. That’s when I feel thrown off.

Do you ever feel the need to do something repeatedly—like checking, counting, or mentally going over what you’ve eaten—to reduce the anxiety you feel when things aren’t planned or measured the way you expect?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, exactly. I mean, I do think things through, probably more than other people might, but I don’t know that I’m repeatedly checking or counting in the way you mean.

I suppose I might go over the day in my head a bit if something feels off, like if a meal wasn’t what I expected or the timing changed, but it’s more… trying to settle myself and understand whether I’m still within what I had planned. It doesn’t feel like a ritual exactly, or like I have to do it a certain number of times. I’m not counting steps or checking the stove or anything like that.

With food, I do like knowing what I’ve had and what I’m going to have, so there is some mental reviewing, but I’ve thought of that as being organized rather than something repetitive. Though maybe I’m splitting hairs. If I can’t measure things the way I expected, I do feel uncomfortable, and then I’ll kind of mentally retrace it. But I wouldn’t say there’s a specific repeated action I have to do to make the anxiety go away.
Outside of your concerns about food and routine, do you find it hard to feel pleasure or satisfaction in things you used to enjoy, even briefly?

I’m not sure I’d say that, no. I mean, I still enjoy things—maybe not always in the uncomplicated way I used to, but I wouldn’t say pleasure has gone missing across the board.

With book club, for example, I do still genuinely like reading the book and hearing what other people think. I like the discussion, especially when someone notices something I completely missed. And at work, there are still moments where solving a problem feels satisfying, in that quiet way—like when the pieces finally line up.

I suppose sometimes I’m distracted or preoccupied enough that it interferes a bit, but I don’t think I’ve lost the ability to enjoy things, even briefly. It’s more that certain situations become complicated if they involve food or uncertainty. Outside of that, I can still feel interested, engaged, pleased with things. So… no, I haven’t really noticed a general numbness or lack of pleasure.
How do you feel if something disrupts your planned routine for the day, like an unexpected event that changes when or what you eat?

I don’t like it. I mean, I can manage it if I have to, but it really throws me off more than I think it probably should.

It’s usually around the food part of the routine that I notice it most. If breakfast is just my usual yogurt, then the day starts in a way that feels simple and predictable. I don’t have to make decisions first thing, and I know where I am, if that makes sense. But if something changes—like I have to leave early, or someone suggests breakfast out, or the timing gets shifted—then I feel this sort of irritation and anxiety together. Not panic exactly, but a very uncomfortable feeling of, “Now the whole day is messy.”

Lunch is a bit different because, honestly, if I’m busy I often just don’t stop for it. That doesn’t feel disruptive to me in the same way; it almost feels easier because I can keep going and not have to rearrange anything. But if someone expects me to eat lunch unexpectedly, or if the day changes so that I can’t keep to what I had in mind, I start thinking ahead to dinner and how to get things back into order.

Dinner is the one I really want measured and contained. By the end of the day I like to feel that I know exactly what I’m having and that it fits with the rest of the day. So if an unexpected event changes what I eat or when I eat, I get tense and preoccupied with how to correct it—not in some dramatic way, but I can’t really relax until I’ve made the day feel orderly again. My doctor seems to think that’s become too tight, and maybe it has, but to me it mostly feels like I’m trying to keep things manageable.
Do you feel anxious or distressed when other parts of your routine are disrupted, not just around food—like if your schedule changes unexpectedly or something doesn’t go exactly as planned?

I’m not sure, actually. I don’t think I react the same way to other schedule changes as I do when it affects meals or what I had planned to eat.

I mean, I like structure generally. I’ve always been someone who keeps a calendar and prefers knowing what’s coming next—part of that is just how I think, and probably my work has reinforced it. If a meeting moves or an errand takes longer than expected, I might be annoyed, but I don’t think I’d call it distressed. I can usually adjust.

Where it starts to feel more uncomfortable is if the change has a knock-on effect, like it pushes back when I’m going to eat or means I can’t do things in the order I expected. Then I get more tense and kind of preoccupied. But if it’s just, say, an appointment time changing or a plan getting rearranged without affecting that part of the day, I don’t think it bothers me beyond normal irritation.

So… I suppose I’m particular, maybe overly particular in some areas, but I haven’t really noticed a broad anxiety about everything needing to go exactly as planned. It’s more specific than that, I think.

When non-food parts of your routine are unexpectedly changed—like a meeting rescheduled or a task taking longer than planned—do you feel more than just mild irritation, such as noticeable anxiety or difficulty focusing on anything else until things feel back in control?

I don’t think so—not in that stronger way you’re describing. If a meeting gets moved, or something at work takes longer than I expected, I can be irritated, certainly. I might mutter about it or feel like, “Well, there goes the plan for the afternoon,” especially because I do like having a sensible order to things.

But I don’t usually get stuck on it to the point where I can’t focus on anything else. I can reshuffle tasks, move something to later, make a new list—honestly, that’s part of what I do for a living, in a way, making systems work when the pieces change. So it’s not pleasant, but it’s manageable.

The place where it gets more difficult is if the schedule change starts to affect the eating part of the day. But if we’re talking strictly non-food things—just a meeting rescheduled, or a phone call running over, or an errand taking longer—I don’t think I’d call it noticeable anxiety. More like annoyance, maybe some tension, and then I adapt.

When unexpected changes happen in your day that aren't related to food—like a sudden change in plans or something not going the way you expected—do you ever feel a strong need to fix or control things in order to feel better, even if it takes extra mental effort or time?

I’m not sure I’d put it as a strong need, no. I do like to straighten things out if plans change, but that may just be how I am. If something unexpected happens, I’ll usually start recalculating in my head—what can move, what needs to be done first, what can be dropped—and sometimes I’ll make another list or redo the timing. But it doesn’t usually feel like I have to control everything or I won’t be okay.

I suppose I do spend mental energy on it, maybe more than some people would. My work has always involved organizing moving parts, so my mind goes there automatically. If a plan changes, I don’t just shrug and improvise; I tend to want a new plan. But once I’ve made one, I can usually continue. I’m not sitting there unable to function until every detail is back exactly the way it was.

So… for non-food things, I’d say it’s more of a preference for order and a habit of problem-solving than a real compulsion to fix things. I can get irritated, and I may fuss with the schedule a bit, but I don’t think it becomes that intense.
When unexpected changes happen in your day that aren't related to food, do you ever feel so unsettled that it's hard to move forward with anything else until things feel back in order?

No, I don’t think so—not really in the sense of being unable to move forward. I can feel thrown off, and I’ll usually want to re-sort things in my head. Like if something takes longer than I expected, I’ll start mentally moving pieces around: “All right, that can wait, this has to happen first, maybe I’ll do that tomorrow.” Sometimes I’ll make a list again, because that calms the situation down for me a bit.

But I wouldn’t say I’m so unsettled that I can’t do anything else until everything is back in order. It’s more that I prefer to have a revised plan before I continue. Once I’ve got even a rough idea of what the new order is, I can usually get on with things.

I suppose other people might see me as a little fussy or overly organized, because I don’t love just winging it. But for non-food parts of the day, it doesn’t usually feel like panic or being completely stuck. More like irritation, a bit of tension, and then I rearrange things and keep going.
When unexpected changes happen in your day that aren't related to food, do you ever feel a strong sense of distress or anxiety that doesn’t go away until everything feels back under control?

I don’t think I’d describe it as a strong sense of distress, no. I mean, I can get tense when things don’t go according to plan, and I’ll usually want to make sense of it quickly—sort of re-map the day in my head. If an appointment moves or a task spills over, I don’t love that. I’ll think, “All right, now what does that affect?” and I may go through the whole chain of it more than I probably need to.

But it doesn’t usually feel like anxiety that stays there until everything is under control. It’s more like I’m uncomfortable with the looseness of it, if that makes sense. I prefer having a plan, and I feel better once I’ve made a new plan, but I’m not sitting there in real distress waiting for every last thing to be settled. I can usually continue, even if I’m a bit annoyed or mentally preoccupied for a little while.

So for non-food things, I’d say no—not that level of distress. More of a “let me reorganize this so it makes sense again” feeling.

And if my clothes don’t feel right, then I can very quickly decide I’ve failed, even if, rationally, I know that’s a harsh way to judge one meal or one day.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences recurrent depressive episodes that may indicate a major depressive disorder, which could be comorbid with an eating disorder or present independently.
doctor.question: Have you ever had periods of time where you felt down or low most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks at a time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about sustained depressed mood for at least two weeks, which is a depressive-symptom screening topic and is not covered by the listed anorexia nervosa symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in that clear, sustained way you’re describing. I’ve had low days, certainly, and sometimes a run of days where I feel more worn down or discouraged than usual. But if you mean most of the day, almost every day, for two weeks or more, I’m not sure I can point to a period like that.

I tend to keep moving through things—work, errands, the usual obligations—so sometimes I’m not even sure I’d notice it properly unless it stopped me. But “down most of the day” sounds more constant than what I experience. Mine feels more like… spells of feeling depleted or frustrated, and then I can still get absorbed in a task or a book or something practical.

So I’d say no, not really. Or at least not that I recognize as a two-week stretch like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in areas of functioning beyond social situations, particularly in occupational or physical health domains, which would help differentiate between eating disorder specifiers and severity levels.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any effects on your work performance or physical health because of your concerns about food and control over your eating?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I still keep up with my analysis work and errands, but I’ve mostly stopped joining friends for meals after book club because it throws off the plan I rely on.

patient.answer:
I think… mostly I’m still functioning, if that’s what you mean. I mean, I still get my analysis work done. I’m careful about deadlines and checking things, and I don’t think anyone at work would say I’m suddenly unreliable or anything like that. And I still manage errands and the practical things—groceries, appointments, paying bills, all of that.

Where it has changed things is more socially, I suppose. After book club, people often want to go for a meal or even just something casual, and I used to go along more easily. Now I’ve mostly stopped doing that, because it throws off the plan I rely on for eating. It’s not that I don’t want to see them, exactly. I do. I like them. But if the timing is different, or I don’t know what the options will be, or it means eating something I hadn’t accounted for, I get very tense about it.

So I wouldn’t say my work has fallen apart or that I can’t take care of myself physically in the day-to-day sense. But it has narrowed things. I’m much more likely to go to book club and then leave, rather than join everyone afterward, because it feels safer to stick to what I had planned.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in areas of functioning beyond social situations, such as in occupational or other important areas, which would support a diagnosis of an eating disorder.
doctor.question: Have your concerns about food, weight, or control over eating caused you significant distress or affected any other important areas of your life, such as your ability to focus at work, take care of personal matters, or engage in hobbies?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I still keep up with my analysis work and errands, but I’ve mostly stopped joining friends for meals after book club because it throws off the plan I rely on.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether food, weight, or eating-control concerns are causing distress or impairing important life areas such as work, personal matters, or hobbies, which most directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes, it has, though I suppose I’d say it’s more… contained than dramatic. I still keep up with my analysis work. I’m not missing deadlines or letting things pile up in some obvious way, and I still manage my errands and the ordinary personal matters—shopping, appointments, bills, that sort of thing.

But it does affect my life around the edges, and maybe those edges are bigger than I like to admit. The main thing is book club. I still go, because I enjoy the books and the discussion, and I don’t want to become someone who stops doing things altogether. But afterward, when people suggest getting a meal or going somewhere for a bite, I’ve mostly stopped joining them.

It’s not because I dislike them. I actually feel a bit sad about it, because I like the conversation afterward too. But eating out like that throws off the plan I rely on, and then I spend the whole time thinking about what I’m supposed to have, what I didn’t account for, whether I’ll feel out of control afterward. So it feels easier and safer to just go home.

So, no, my work and errands haven’t really suffered in a visible way. But socially, yes—it’s narrowed what I’m willing to do.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concerns about food and control meet criteria for Anorexia Nervosa (F50.00) versus Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (F42), by clarifying whether the behaviors are primarily driven by a preoccupation with body shape and weight, or by intrusive, unwanted thoughts and compulsions.
doctor.question: Do you feel driven to control your eating because of intrusive, unwanted thoughts about food or weight, or do you do it more because you feel anxious or uncomfortable if things aren’t planned and measured just right?

target_item.name: Restrictive_Intake
target_item.manifestation: I came in because my doctor seems concerned that my meal planning has gotten too tight, though to me it just feels like keeping breakfast to yogurt, skipping lunch if I’m busy, and making a very measured dinner so the day stays orderly.
target_item.reason: The question is most directly about the drive to control eating through planning and measuring food intake, which matches the restrictive intake pattern described in the profile.

patient.answer:
I think it’s more the second thing, honestly. I wouldn’t say it’s like intrusive thoughts in the sense of thoughts barging in that feel separate from me, if that makes sense. It’s more that if the day isn’t planned around food in a fairly exact way, I feel unsettled—like I’ve lost the structure of the day.

I came in because my doctor seems concerned that my meal planning has gotten too tight. To me, it still feels sort of practical and orderly. Breakfast is usually just yogurt, because it’s simple and I know what it is. If I’m busy, lunch can get skipped, which doesn’t feel like a big decision at the time—it’s more that I’m working or out doing things and it seems easier not to interrupt everything. Then dinner is very measured, because by then I want the day to feel… contained, I suppose. Like I can account for it.

So no, I don’t experience it as unwanted thoughts attacking me exactly. It’s more that I feel anxious or uncomfortable when I can’t keep it planned and measured properly. That’s when I feel thrown off.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences compulsive behaviors or mental acts in response to anxiety about food or weight, which could indicate OCD rather than an eating disorder alone.
doctor.question: Do you ever feel the need to do something repeatedly—like checking, counting, or mentally going over what you’ve eaten—to reduce the anxiety you feel when things aren’t planned or measured the way you expect?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about repetitive compulsive behaviors such as checking, counting, or mentally reviewing intake to reduce anxiety, which is not covered by the provided anorexia nervosa symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, exactly. I mean, I do think things through, probably more than other people might, but I don’t know that I’m repeatedly checking or counting in the way you mean.

I suppose I might go over the day in my head a bit if something feels off, like if a meal wasn’t what I expected or the timing changed, but it’s more… trying to settle myself and understand whether I’m still within what I had planned. It doesn’t feel like a ritual exactly, or like I have to do it a certain number of times. I’m not counting steps or checking the stove or anything like that.

With food, I do like knowing what I’ve had and what I’m going to have, so there is some mental reviewing, but I’ve thought of that as being organized rather than something repetitive. Though maybe I’m splitting hairs. If I can’t measure things the way I expected, I do feel uncomfortable, and then I’ll kind of mentally retrace it. But I wouldn’t say there’s a specific repeated action I have to do to make the anxiety go away.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences distress or impairment outside of meal planning that could indicate a mood disorder (F42 vs. F50.00).
doctor.question: Outside of your concerns about food and routine, do you find it hard to feel pleasure or satisfaction in things you used to enjoy, even briefly?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of pleasure or satisfaction in previously enjoyed activities, which is not covered by the provided anorexia nervosa symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d say that, no. I mean, I still enjoy things—maybe not always in the uncomplicated way I used to, but I wouldn’t say pleasure has gone missing across the board.

With book club, for example, I do still genuinely like reading the book and hearing what other people think. I like the discussion, especially when someone notices something I completely missed. And at work, there are still moments where solving a problem feels satisfying, in that quiet way—like when the pieces finally line up.

I suppose sometimes I’m distracted or preoccupied enough that it interferes a bit, but I don’t think I’ve lost the ability to enjoy things, even briefly. It’s more that certain situations become complicated if they involve food or uncertainty. Outside of that, I can still feel interested, engaged, pleased with things. So… no, I haven’t really noticed a general numbness or lack of pleasure.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant anxiety or distress specifically when routines or food-related plans are disrupted, which would help distinguish between an eating disorder (F50.00) and OCD-related anxiety (F42).
doctor.question: How do you feel if something disrupts your planned routine for the day, like an unexpected event that changes when or what you eat?

target_item.name: Restrictive_Intake
target_item.manifestation: I came in because my doctor seems concerned that my meal planning has gotten too tight, though to me it just feels like keeping breakfast to yogurt, skipping lunch if I’m busy, and making a very measured dinner so the day stays orderly.
target_item.reason: The question asks about how disruptions to the patient’s planned eating routine affect her, which is most directly tied to her restrictive, tightly planned intake pattern.

patient.answer:
I don’t like it. I mean, I can manage it if I have to, but it really throws me off more than I think it probably should.

It’s usually around the food part of the routine that I notice it most. If breakfast is just my usual yogurt, then the day starts in a way that feels simple and predictable. I don’t have to make decisions first thing, and I know where I am, if that makes sense. But if something changes—like I have to leave early, or someone suggests breakfast out, or the timing gets shifted—then I feel this sort of irritation and anxiety together. Not panic exactly, but a very uncomfortable feeling of, “Now the whole day is messy.”

Lunch is a bit different because, honestly, if I’m busy I often just don’t stop for it. That doesn’t feel disruptive to me in the same way; it almost feels easier because I can keep going and not have to rearrange anything. But if someone expects me to eat lunch unexpectedly, or if the day changes so that I can’t keep to what I had in mind, I start thinking ahead to dinner and how to get things back into order.

Dinner is the one I really want measured and contained. By the end of the day I like to feel that I know exactly what I’m having and that it fits with the rest of the day. So if an unexpected event changes what I eat or when I eat, I get tense and preoccupied with how to correct it—not in some dramatic way, but I can’t really relax until I’ve made the day feel orderly again. My doctor seems to think that’s become too tight, and maybe it has, but to me it mostly feels like I’m trying to keep things manageable.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant anxiety or distress in response to disruptions in routine that go beyond food-related concerns, which could indicate features of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious or distressed when other parts of your routine are disrupted, not just around food—like if your schedule changes unexpectedly or something doesn’t go exactly as planned?

target_item.reason: The question asks about distress when non-food routines or schedules are disrupted, but the provided symptom profile only covers food-related restriction, weight/shape concerns, low weight recognition, and related social impairment.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure, actually. I don’t think I react the same way to other schedule changes as I do when it affects meals or what I had planned to eat.

I mean, I like structure generally. I’ve always been someone who keeps a calendar and prefers knowing what’s coming next—part of that is just how I think, and probably my work has reinforced it. If a meeting moves or an errand takes longer than expected, I might be annoyed, but I don’t think I’d call it distressed. I can usually adjust.

Where it starts to feel more uncomfortable is if the change has a knock-on effect, like it pushes back when I’m going to eat or means I can’t do things in the order I expected. Then I get more tense and kind of preoccupied. But if it’s just, say, an appointment time changing or a plan getting rearranged without affecting that part of the day, I don’t think it bothers me beyond normal irritation.

So… I suppose I’m particular, maybe overly particular in some areas, but I haven’t really noticed a broad anxiety about everything needing to go exactly as planned. It’s more specific than that, I think.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant anxiety or distress specifically when non-food-related routines are disrupted, beyond normal irritation, which would help differentiate between the two diagnostic candidates.
doctor.question: When non-food parts of your routine are unexpectedly changed—like a meeting rescheduled or a task taking longer than planned—do you feel more than just mild irritation, such as noticeable anxiety or difficulty focusing on anything else until things feel back in control?

target_item.reason: The question is about anxiety or difficulty focusing when non-food routines are disrupted, which is not covered by the listed anorexia nervosa symptom profiles. The available items focus on food restriction, low weight, fear of weight gain, body image, non-recognition of low weight seriousness, and food-related functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so—not in that stronger way you’re describing. If a meeting gets moved, or something at work takes longer than I expected, I can be irritated, certainly. I might mutter about it or feel like, “Well, there goes the plan for the afternoon,” especially because I do like having a sensible order to things.

But I don’t usually get stuck on it to the point where I can’t focus on anything else. I can reshuffle tasks, move something to later, make a new list—honestly, that’s part of what I do for a living, in a way, making systems work when the pieces change. So it’s not pleasant, but it’s manageable.

The place where it gets more difficult is if the schedule change starts to affect the eating part of the day. But if we’re talking strictly non-food things—just a meeting rescheduled, or a phone call running over, or an errand taking longer—I don’t think I’d call it noticeable anxiety. More like annoyance, maybe some tension, and then I adapt.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences clinically significant anxiety or distress in response to disruptions in non-food-related routines, which could support a diagnosis of OCD rather than an eating disorder alone.
doctor.question: When unexpected changes happen in your day that aren't related to food—like a sudden change in plans or something not going the way you expected—do you ever feel a strong need to fix or control things in order to feel better, even if it takes extra mental effort or time?

target_item.reason: The question is about a strong need for control or rigidity in non-food-related routine changes, which is not covered by the listed anorexia nervosa symptom profiles. The available profiles focus on restrictive intake, low weight, fear of weight gain, body image disturbance, lack of recognition of low-weight seriousness, and functional impairment around meals.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d put it as a strong need, no. I do like to straighten things out if plans change, but that may just be how I am. If something unexpected happens, I’ll usually start recalculating in my head—what can move, what needs to be done first, what can be dropped—and sometimes I’ll make another list or redo the timing. But it doesn’t usually feel like I have to control everything or I won’t be okay.

I suppose I do spend mental energy on it, maybe more than some people would. My work has always involved organizing moving parts, so my mind goes there automatically. If a plan changes, I don’t just shrug and improvise; I tend to want a new plan. But once I’ve made one, I can usually continue. I’m not sitting there unable to function until every detail is back exactly the way it was.

So… for non-food things, I’d say it’s more of a preference for order and a habit of problem-solving than a real compulsion to fix things. I can get irritated, and I may fuss with the schedule a bit, but I don’t think it becomes that intense.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in areas outside of food-related routines when routines are disrupted, which would help differentiate between F50.00 (Anorexia Nervosa) and F42 (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder).
doctor.question: When unexpected changes happen in your day that aren't related to food, do you ever feel so unsettled that it's hard to move forward with anything else until things feel back in order?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about distress or difficulty moving forward after unexpected non-food-related routine changes, which is not covered by the provided anorexia nervosa symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so—not really in the sense of being unable to move forward. I can feel thrown off, and I’ll usually want to re-sort things in my head. Like if something takes longer than I expected, I’ll start mentally moving pieces around: “All right, that can wait, this has to happen first, maybe I’ll do that tomorrow.” Sometimes I’ll make a list again, because that calms the situation down for me a bit.

But I wouldn’t say I’m so unsettled that I can’t do anything else until everything is back in order. It’s more that I prefer to have a revised plan before I continue. Once I’ve got even a rough idea of what the new order is, I can usually get on with things.

I suppose other people might see me as a little fussy or overly organized, because I don’t love just winging it. But for non-food parts of the day, it doesn’t usually feel like panic or being completely stuck. More like irritation, a bit of tension, and then I rearrange things and keep going.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant anxiety or distress specifically related to disruptions in non-food routines, which could indicate broader obsessive-compulsive tendencies beyond eating behaviors.
doctor.question: When unexpected changes happen in your day that aren't related to food, do you ever feel a strong sense of distress or anxiety that doesn’t go away until everything feels back under control?

patient.answer:
I don’t think I’d describe it as a strong sense of distress, no. I mean, I can get tense when things don’t go according to plan, and I’ll usually want to make sense of it quickly—sort of re-map the day in my head. If an appointment moves or a task spills over, I don’t love that. I’ll think, “All right, now what does that affect?” and I may go through the whole chain of it more than I probably need to.

But it doesn’t usually feel like anxiety that stays there until everything is under control. It’s more like I’m uncomfortable with the looseness of it, if that makes sense. I prefer having a plan, and I feel better once I’ve made a new plan, but I’m not sitting there in real distress waiting for every last thing to be settled. I can usually continue, even if I’m a bit annoyed or mentally preoccupied for a little while.

So for non-food things, I’d say no—not that level of distress. More of a “let me reorganize this so it makes sense again” feeling.
